Well balanced finite volume schemes for shallow water equations on manifolds

Journal: Applied Mathematics and Computation
Michele Giuliano Carlino Email: michele-giuliano.carlino@inria.fr Corresponding author: Corresponding author Address: Inria, Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Bordeaux INP, IMB, UMR 5251, 200 Avenue de la Vieille Tour, 33405 Talence cedex, France    Elena Gaburro Email: elena.gaburro@inria.fr Address: Inria, Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Bordeaux INP, IMB, UMR 5251, 200 Avenue de la Vieille Tour, 33405 Talence cedex, France
Abstract

In this paper we propose a novel second-order accurate well balanced scheme for shallow water equations in general covariant coordinates over manifolds. In our approach, once the gravitational field is defined for the specific case, one equipotential surface is detected and parametrized by a frame of general covariant coordinates. This surface is the manifold whose covariant parametrization induces a metric tensor. The model is then re-written in a hyperbolic form with a tuple of conserved variables composed both of the evolving physical quantities and the metric coefficients. This formulation allows the numerical scheme to automatically compute the curvature of the manifold as long as the physical variables are evolved.

In a classical well balanced formulation, the knowledge of a given equilibrium is exploited for evolving the specific state seen as the sum of the equilibrium and the fluctuations of the state around the equilibrium itself. On the contrary, the numerical approach proposed here is automatically well balanced for the water at rest solution (defined by zero velocity and constant free surface) for general manifolds without having to exploit the exact equilibrium profile during the computation. In particular, this numerical strategy allows to preserve the accuracy of the water at rest equilibrium at machine precision and on large timescales, even for non-smooth bottom topographies. As a matter of fact, the proposed local polynomial reconstruction, needed at each time step by the scheme for evolving the state, is built in order to automatically cancel any numerical error committed for describing jumps in the bathymetry. As a further effect, also out of the equilibrium, the typical spurious non-physical oscillations of the recovered numerical solution in a neighborhood of the discontinuities are healed. Thus, once the information on both the bathymetry and the metric of the manifold are properly collected in the flux terms and in the nonconservative products, the resulting numerical strategy turns out to be more accurate in finding also non-equilibrium solutions.

Numerical results close the work. After having proved that the scheme is second-order accurate, we test the recovery of the water at rest equilibrium at machine precision for different bottom topographies (eventually discontinuous) with various metric on very long simulation times. In particular, after having considered smooth bathymetries with compact support, we relax the assumption on the continuity of water at rest equilibrium with discontinuous bathymetries disturbed by a white noise.

Keywords: 
Hyperbolic Partial Differential Equations , Shallow Water equations (SW) , Finite Volume methods (FV) , Well Balanced methods (WB) , General Covariant coordinates , Manifold

1 Introduction

The goal of this article consists in developing a second-order accurate scheme for Shallow Water (SW) equations in General Covariant Coordinates (GCCs) over a manifold. The proposed scheme is able to preserve the special equilibrium of water at rest (i.e. zero velocity and constant free surface) over long times. The considered physical model, discretized by the scheme, takes into account the particular shape of the gravitational field leading the dynamics of the movement of the fluid of the test case in consideration.

SW equations have been a useful tool for describing various phenomena related to fluid geophysics, from the study of flows in a lake to the movement of water in a river [56, 87, 32, 39, 50], to appropriately describing meteorological [49, 51] or oceanic [48, 25] phenomena over long distances or providing a useful risk analysis tool for avalanches [42] or tsunamis [70]. Although all of these physical phenomena respond to the same type of mathematical description, the input datum of the gravitational field can change with respect to the spatial scale and with respect to the bottom topography under consideration [73, 8, 72]. Indeed, starting with the shallow water assumption for which fluid particles have negligible motion along the gravitational field lines [65] (shallow water hypothesis), consider an immersed manifold that is a significant surface perpendicular to the gravitational field lines. From the manifold, a certain metric is deduced that allows us to describe the differential operator of SW equations. Such an operator will then be strongly dependent on the metric, thus on the curvature of the manifold, and will change from case to case. Concrete examples may be those involving the fluid dynamic study of a lake, in which gravity can be modeled as perpendicular to a horizontal plane, or oceanic dynamics that take into account a spherical distribution of gravity [85, 55, 2, 6] up to more detailed descriptions that, accounting for the different local mass placement of the planet, consider gravity as a field that varies in modulus and direction with respect to the physical-geographical characteristics of the Earth’s geoid [75, 74].

The starting mathematical model of this paper thus considers as input the metric description of the manifold, and once this is defined as initial datum, it is appropriately integrated into the differential operator leading to a hyperbolic differential system that evolves the solution with respect to the geometric characteristics of the manifold itself in an autonomous way.

In general, for small variations in the bathymetry, also for large distances (e.g. oceanic distances), the fluid depth is evaluated in vertical direction, which does not necessarily coincide with the direction of the gravitational forces. This violates the previously stated shallow water hypothesis. Although such an approximation might seem reasonable with respect to the variation of the gravitational field perpendicular to a certain surface, Bachini and Putti in [5] have shown that the SW equations resulting i) from the integration of the Navier-Stokes equations along gravitational field lines and ii) along the vertical reference line lead to significantly different numerical results for the same physical phenomenon, even for bathymetries that vary very slightly in space. Concerning spherical gravitational field, similar differences have been recorded also by Chow in [24]. Therefore, for a numerical output to be as accurate as possible, the shape of the gravitational field must be properly accounted for in the mathematical model describing a certain phenomenon.

In addition to the SW classical model, in Cartesian coordinates, in literature it is possible to find SW models that are described by only one fixed frame of general covariant coordinates, for example see [20, 2] for spherical coordinates. A particular case is given by Baldauf in [6], from which our work starts (see Sec. 2). In this last cited article, despite a general formulation in a general covariant frame is provided for describing the shallow water system, all the geometrical features of the accounted spherical and elliptical manifolds are considered in the system as input data, included the curvatures. Instead, the approach we propose here is different, because the hyperbolic system we formulate, in addition to the physical quantities, only needs the metric to be given in input (and the metric will be part of the set of conserved variables). Then, once the metric is defined, the system automatically computes all the other geometric terms describing the curvature of the manifold (for example the Christoffel symbols). So, at the same time, our model evolves the conserved physical variables and computes the specific geometric features of the manifold, being thus more general and flexible.

This approach is strongly inspired by the work by Gaburro, Dumbser & Castro in [36]. Although this paper deals with numerical schemes on general relativity, basically the gravitational terms in fixed backgrounds are not considered in algebraic form as a source term but, through the use of nonconservative terms, they are expressed as a function of the spatial derivatives of appropriate conserved variables. Equivalently in our context, the terms related to the spatial derivatives in general covariant coordinates of the covariant formulation of the metric define the nonconservative terms of the hyperbolic system. Thus, the tuple of conserved variable is composed not only of the physical variables of the system but also of the geometric description of the manifold. The advantage of this formulation is that, therefore, the spatial curvature is calculated discretely in a system-autonomous form and taken into account in the evolution of physics.

This is made possible by considering a general covariant formulation of the problem. In the literature also another approach via Local Covariant Coordinates (LCC) can be found (e.g. see [6, 31, 2]). One advantage of LCC strategy is that eventual critical points for the metric (i.e. those points of the computational domain over which the determinant of the metric vanishes, e.g. the poles onto a sphere in classical longitudinal-latitudinal spherical mapping) are avoided because any cell (also those containing these pathological points) are mapped into a reference system where the numerical solution is recovered. However, the numerical scheme that is constructed increases in complexity because this reference map is added to the one that parameterizes the manifold in the computational domain. So, specific strategies need to be employed to recover the possible continuity of the solution or alternatively the conservativity of the numerical fluxes. Moreover, in a local covariant coordinates approach it becomes more challenging to deal with discontinuous bathymetry because the local map along the jumps usually becomes singular unless special ad hoc constructed numerical manipulations are employed [81].

Besides, the objective of preserving over long simulation times one or more equilibria of the model, can be assessed via the well balancing feature of the numerical method. When a scheme is well balanced, it eliminates spurious numerical modes, it reduces the numerical dissipation and small-scale phenomena may be more evident on larger scales. In [12], Bermudez and Vazquez use shallow water system to well balance it with respect to water at rest equilibrium in a rigorous mathematical fashion. Afterwards, concerning this topic, the literature has expanded; as examples we cite [57, 66, 41, 68, 14, 4, 76, 17, 52, 22, 19, 38, 35, 54, 45, 78, 10, 40, 46, 9]. A comprehensive literature review on the topic is given by Castro & Parés in [21]. With respect to well balancing for SW, in addition, [59, 61, 62, 69, 53, 86, 1] can be cited.

A crucial aspect of this article is to relax the continuity hypothesis of the solution. Typically, equilibrium is considered to be a smooth steady solution. But in general this assumption cannot be considered. In practical situations it is not always possible to detect the bathymetry in continuous form. Therefore, even where the bathymetry is at least Lipshitz-continuous, it is discretized as discontinuous. For that reason, the depth of the fluid would also be discontinuous. In this paper we propose a way such that any numerical error due to jumps in bathymetry automatically cancels when the solution evolves. This approach not only preserves the water at rest equilibrium but also allows us to recover a numerical solution out the equilibrium that is not affected by any bad approximations of jumps in the bottom.

The paper is organized as follows. The original shallow water model on manifolds in general covariant coordinates is presented in Sec. 2. In this section the hyperbolic system takes in input the metric as well as all the geometrical features of the manifold. After some physical remarks in order to properly define the meaning of the manifold in this context, in Sec. 2.1 the water at rest equilibrium is introduced with respect to a general covariant frame. Afterwards, Sec. 3 is devoted to the derivation of the final formulation of the novel shallow water governing model in general covariant coordinates only depending on the metric. In particular, the new hyperbolic system, formally presented in Sec. 3.1, is able to evolve the physical variables and, at the same time, to automatically compute the geometrical features of the manifold. The adopted numerical scheme is described in Sec. 4 and its well balanced formulation is analysed in Sec. 5. Numerical validations are in Sec. 6. The paper is closed by conclusions and future perspectives in Sec. 7.

2 Shallow water equations on manifolds in general covariant coordinates

The considered differential system for shallow water equations on an arbitrary dd-dimensional manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} (with d=1,2d=1,2) in general covariant coordinates is originally introduced in [6] by Baldauf. For any nonnegative time tt and for any GCC 𝐱=(x1,x2)\mathbf{x}=(x^{1},x^{2}) in the reference domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathds{R}^{d}, it reads

∂h∂t+∇jmj\displaystyle\frac{\partial h}{\partial t}+\nabla_{j}m^{j} =0,\displaystyle=0, (1a)
∂mi∂t+∇jTi​j\displaystyle\frac{\partial m^{i}}{\partial t}+\nabla_{j}T^{ij} =Si,\displaystyle=S^{i}, (1b)

for i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. In the above system and in the sequel the Einstein notation for sum on repeated indexes (both superscript and subscript) is used, with exception if they are written in round brackets. In system (1), the evolving unknowns in time are the fluid depth hh (in the conservation of the mass (1a)) and the mass fluxes mi=h​uim^{i}=hu^{i} (in the balance of the momentum (1b)), with uiu^{i} representing the two velocity components of the fluid with respect to the principal directions defined by the generalized coordinates xix^{i}, see Fig. 1. In the momentum equation in (1), the flux is defined by the stress tensor

Ti​j=mi​mjh+12​g​h2​γi​j,T^{ij}=\frac{m^{i}m^{j}}{h}+\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\gamma^{ij}, (2)

composed of the sum between a kinetic and a pressure component. In the latter, the gravitational constant gg and the contravariant metric tensor γi​j\gamma^{ij} intervene. The source term SiS^{i} is defined as

Si=−ghγi​j∂xjb,S^{i}=-gh\gamma^{ij}\partial_{x^{j}}b, (3)

where bb is the bathymetry. In the source term (3) any contribution from Coriolis, bottom-friction or viscous forces is neglected. The treatment of these further terms depends on the particular test case one wishes to study and is beyond the scope of this article. The reader is referred to [80, 15, 44, 6, 31] for more specific instances in which the contributions deduced from the physics of the case under consideration are added to the only gravitational contribution in (3).
Since the covariant derivative ∇j\nabla_{j} expands in the sum of the derivatives with respect to the covariant coordinate xjx^{j} and the additional metric terms that account for the curvature of the manifold via Christoffel symbols, equations (1) can be equivalently rewritten as

∂h∂t+∂mj∂xj+Γj​kj​mk\displaystyle\frac{\partial h}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial m^{j}}{\partial x^{j}}+\Gamma^{j}_{jk}m^{k} =0,\displaystyle=0, (4a)
∂mi∂t+∂Ti​j∂xj+Γj​ki​Tk​j+Γj​kj​Ti​k\displaystyle\frac{\partial m^{i}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial T^{ij}}{\partial x^{j}}+\Gamma^{i}_{jk}T^{kj}+\Gamma^{j}_{jk}T^{ik} =Si.\displaystyle=S^{i}. (4b)

By definition, the Christoffel symbol Γj​ki\Gamma^{i}_{jk} of second kind is

Γj​ki=12​γi​m​(∂γk​m∂xj+∂γj​m∂xk−∂γj​k∂xm),\Gamma^{i}_{jk}=\frac{1}{2}\gamma^{im}\bigg(\frac{\partial\gamma_{km}}{\partial x^{j}}+\frac{\partial\gamma_{jm}}{\partial x^{k}}-\frac{\partial\gamma_{jk}}{\partial x^{m}}\bigg), (5)

where γi​j\gamma_{ij} is the covariant representation of the metric tensor. Thus, it is the inverse of the contravariant metric γi​j\gamma^{ij}, i.e. γi​j​γj​k=δki\gamma^{ij}\gamma_{jk}=\delta^{i}_{k}, with δki\delta^{i}_{k} the Kronecker symbol.
Due to the definition of the gravitational contribution in the source term (3), the manifold over which system (4) is solved has to be an equipotential surface [6]. Extension to non equipotential manifolds for SW in GCC (1) are discussed by Staniforth in [73]. As a direct consequence, the gravitational field 𝐠\mathbf{g} (whose modulus is taken constantly equal to gg in this paper) is perpendicular to the manifold (because it is normal to any equipotential surface). Thus, the height hh is defined as the length of the gravitational field line conducted from the free surface η=h+b\eta=h+b of the fluid to the bottom, as it is sketched in Fig. 1.

Remark 2.1.

In this paper, the fluid depth hh, velocity component uiu^{i} (or the relative mass flux mim^{i}), for i=1,2i=1,2, and the bathymetry bb are said physical quantities; all terms involving the metric tensor (in contravariant or covariant form) are called metric quantities.

2.1 The water at rest equilibria at continuum level

One goal of this article is to develop a well balanced numerical scheme for the shallow water equations in general covariant coordinates. In particular, the well-balancing of the method is built with respect to the special equilibrium of water at rest. Such an equilibrium is one possible solution in the uncountable set of solutions that satisfy the following proposition.

Proposition 2.1 (Frame-free features of water at rest equilibria).

For problem (4) with a nonsingular metric γi​j\gamma^{ij} and an assigned bathymetry bb, the water at rest equilibrium consists in a fluid depth hh and a couple of velocity components (u1,u2)(u^{1},u^{2}) such that

η=h+b≡const. \eta=h+b\equiv\text{const. } (6a)
and
u1=u2≡0,u^{1}=u^{2}\equiv 0, (6b)

for any positive time tt and for any 𝐱∈Ω\mathbf{x}\in\Omega.

Proof.

Since the velocity components uiu^{i} vanish, mass fluxes mim^{i} are zero. Consequently, the mass conservation equation (4a) is automatically satisfied. Moreover, condition (6b) implies that the stress tensor (2) reduces just to its pressure component

Ti​j=12​g​h2​γi​j.T^{ij}=\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\gamma^{ij}. (7)

By applying the chain rule for deriving (7) w.r.t. to xjx^{j}, equations (4b) turn into

g​γi​j​∂h∂xj+12​g​h2​γi​j+Γj​ki​(12​g​h2​γk​j)+Γj​kj​(12​g​h2​γi​k)=−g​h​γi​j​∂b∂xj.g\gamma^{ij}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x^{j}}+\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\gamma^{ij}+\Gamma^{i}_{jk}\bigg(\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\gamma^{kj}\bigg)+\Gamma^{j}_{jk}\bigg(\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\gamma^{ik}\bigg)=-gh\gamma^{ij}\frac{\partial b}{\partial x^{j}}. (8)

Condition (6a) implies that ∂xj(h+b)=0\partial_{x^{j}}(h+b)=0, for j=1,2j=1,2. Consequently, equations (8) read

12​g​h2​(∂γi​j∂xj+Γj​ki​γk​j+Γj​kj​γi​k)=0,∀i∈{1,2}.\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\bigg(\frac{\partial\gamma^{ij}}{\partial x^{j}}+\Gamma^{i}_{jk}\gamma^{kj}+\Gamma^{j}_{jk}\gamma^{ik}\bigg)=0,\quad\forall i\in\{1,2\}. (9)

The quantity into brackets in the left hand side of (9) is the covariant derivative of the metric tensor γi​j\gamma^{ij} w.r.t. to xjx^{j}, i.e. ∇jγi​j\nabla_{j}\gamma^{ij}. Since the connection is chosen to have zero covariant derivative of the metric (in order to allow parallel transport operations which preserve angles and lengths, see Sec. 3.1 of [84]), equations (9) are verified. As a consequence, the momentum conservation equations (4b) are satisfied as well.
Finally, it is proved that equilibrium (6) of water at rest is a solution for SW equations in GCC (4) for any nonsingular metric. ∎

Remark 2.2.

For equilibrium of Prop. 2.1, condition (6a) on constant free surface η\eta has to be intended with respect to the frame of general covariant coordinates 𝐱=(x1,x2)\mathbf{x}=(x^{1},x^{2}). This definition, thus, is still related to the shape of the gravitational field. For example, let us consider two cases of a lake and of an ocean. In the former, the gravitational field can be approximated to be parallel to the vertical direction, in the latter the gravitational field is defined addressing to the center of a spheric planet of radius RR. Consequently the natural frames of the two cases are Cartesian (𝐱=(x,y)\mathbf{x}=(x,y), with xx and yy coordinates measuring lengths) and spherical (𝐱=(θ,φ)\mathbf{x}=(\theta,\varphi), with θ\theta and φ\varphi latitudinal and longitudinal angles), respectively. For the lake, condition (6a) means that the free surface is constant with respect to Cartesian coordinates (x,y)(x,y) (see Fig. 2(a)), while for the ocean it is intended constant with respect to the angles (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi) but not with respect to the related Cartesian coordinates given by (R​cos⁡(θ)​cos⁡(φ),R​sin⁡(θ)​cos⁡(φ))(R\cos(\theta)\cos(\varphi),R\sin(\theta)\cos(\varphi)) (see Fig. 2(b)).

3 Derivation and final formulation of the novel SW governing model in general covariant coordinates with dependence only on the metric

In this section, we reformulate the original shallow water model (1) in order to make it independent of the physical general covariant reference frame. In particular, our objective consists in giving to the system the metric as input data such that it automatically evolves the physical variables and computes the geometrical features of the manifolds by the only information provided by the metric itself.

In order to numerically solve problem (4), we have re-written it in the first-order hyperbolic form

𝐐t+∇⋅𝐅⁡(𝐐)+𝐁⁡(𝐐)⋅∇𝐐=𝟎,𝐱=(x1,x2)∈Ω⊂ℝd,t∈[0,T],\mathbf{Q}_{t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q})+\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{Q})\cdot\nabla\mathbf{Q}=\boldsymbol{0},\quad\mathbf{x}=(x^{1},x^{2})\in\Omega\subset\mathds{R}^{d},\quad t\in[0,T], (10)

where 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the vector space in the computational domain Ω\Omega of dimension d=1,2d=1,2 and tt is time from 0 to final time T>0T>0. The state 𝐐\mathbf{Q} (collecting the conserved variables of the equations) is defined in the space of admissible states Ω𝐐∈ℝm\Omega_{\mathbf{Q}}\in\mathds{R}^{m}. The nonlinear flux tensor and the nonlinear matrix of nonconservative terms are 𝐅⁡(𝐐)\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q}) and 𝐁⁡(𝐐)\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{Q}), respectively. Their definitions strictly depend on the space dimension dd. In particular, when Ω\Omega is a two-dimensional set, they read 𝐅⁡(𝐐)=(𝐟1​(𝐐),𝐟2​(𝐐))\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q})=(\mathbf{f}_{1}(\mathbf{Q}),\mathbf{f}_{2}(\mathbf{Q})) and 𝐁⁡(𝐐)=(𝐁1​(𝐐),𝐁2​(𝐐))\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{Q})=(\mathbf{B}_{1}(\mathbf{Q}),\mathbf{B}_{2}(\mathbf{Q})), with 𝐟1,𝐟2∈ℝm\mathbf{f}_{1},\mathbf{f}_{2}\in\mathds{R}^{m} and 𝐁1,𝐁2∈ℝm×m\mathbf{B}_{1},\mathbf{B}_{2}\in\mathds{R}^{m\times m}. Otherwise, they reduce to 𝐅​(𝐐)=𝐟i​(𝐐)\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q})=\mathbf{f}_{i}(\mathbf{Q}) and 𝐁​(𝐐)=𝐁i​(𝐐)\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{Q})=\mathbf{B}_{i}(\mathbf{Q}) if PDE (10) is solved along one principal direction led by xix_{i}, with i=1,2i=1,2. System (10) is hyperbolic if, for any nonzero directions 𝐧=(n1,n2)\mathbf{n}=(n^{1},n^{2}), matrix 𝐀=(∂𝐅/∂𝐐+𝐁⁡(𝐐))⋅𝐧\mathbf{A}=(\partial\mathbf{F}/\partial\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{Q}))\cdot\mathbf{n} has a full real spectrum and its eigenvectors define a complete basis for ℝm\mathds{R}^{m}.

3.1 Derivation of the governing model

System (10) is built by splitting all derivatives of the physical quantities from the derivatives of metric terms, as done, for example, in step (8) of the proof of Prop. 2.1.
In order to consider a full covariant system, indexes of contravariant metric tensor γi​j\gamma^{ij} have to be lowered for obtaining its covariant representation γi​j\gamma_{ij}. The former tensor is the inverse of the latter one and both are symmetric in ℝ2×2\mathds{R}^{2\times 2}. Let α:{1,2}2→{1,2}2\alpha:\{1,2\}^{2}\rightarrow\{1,2\}^{2} be a discrete map defined as α⁡(i,j)=(3−i,3−j)\alpha(i,j)=(3-i,3-j). Given an index equal to either 1 or 2, map α\alpha exchanges its value with the only other possible one (e.g. α⁡(1,2)=(2,1)\alpha(1,2)=(2,1); α⁡(2,2)=(1,1)\alpha(2,2)=(1,1)). Moreover, tensor Gi​j=2​δi​j−1G_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-1 is defined. Since it holds

[γi​j]=1γ​[γ22−γ12−γ12γ11],[\gamma^{ij}]=\frac{1}{\gamma}\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{22}&-\gamma_{12}\\ -\gamma_{12}&\gamma_{11}\end{bmatrix}, (11)

with γ=det[γi​j]=γ11​γ22−γ122\gamma=\det[\gamma_{ij}]=\gamma_{11}\gamma_{22}-\gamma_{12}^{2}, expression (11) in index representation is

γi​j=1γ​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i,j)).\gamma^{ij}=\frac{1}{\gamma}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(i,j))}. (12)

After having applied the chain rule and due to (12), the flux term in the momentum equilibrium (4b) is rewritten as

∂∂xj​Ti​j\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}T^{ij} =∂∂xj​(mi​mjh)+g​h​γi​j​∂∂xj​h+12​g​h2​∂∂xj​γi​j\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\bigg(\frac{m^{i}m^{j}}{h}\bigg)+gh\gamma^{ij}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}h+\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\gamma^{ij} (13)
=∂∂xj​(mi​mjh)+g​hγ​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i,j))​∂∂xj​h+12​g​h2​∂∂xj​(1γ​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i,j))).\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\bigg(\frac{m^{i}m^{j}}{h}\bigg)+\frac{gh}{\gamma}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(i,j))}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}h+\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\bigg(\frac{1}{\gamma}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(i,j))}\bigg).

For a generic function f∈C1​(Ω)f\in C^{1}(\Omega), it holds

∂∂xkfγ=1γ∂∂xkf−fγ2γ22∂∂xkγ11+2​fγ2γ12∂∂xkγ12−fγ2γ11∂∂xkγ22,k=1,2.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\frac{f}{\gamma}=\frac{1}{\gamma}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}f-\frac{f}{\gamma^{2}}\gamma_{22}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{11}+\frac{2f}{\gamma^{2}}\gamma_{12}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{12}-\frac{f}{\gamma^{2}}\gamma_{11}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{22},\quad k=1,2. (14)

Consequently, the last term in (13) turns into

12​g​h2​∂∂xj​(G(i​j)γ​γ(α⁡(i,j)))=g​h22​γ​[∂∂xj​(G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i​j)))−γ22​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i​j))​∂∂xj​γ11+2​γ12​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i​j))​∂∂xj​γ12−G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i​j))​γ22​∂∂xj​γ22].\frac{1}{2}gh^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\bigg(\frac{G_{(ij)}}{\gamma}\gamma_{(\alpha(i,j))}\bigg)=\frac{gh^{2}}{2\gamma}\bigg[\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}(G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(ij))})-\gamma_{22}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(ij))}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\gamma_{11}+2\gamma_{12}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(ij))}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\gamma_{12}-G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(ij))}\gamma_{22}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\gamma_{22}\bigg]. (15)

Relation (12) also allows to rewrite the source term in (4b) as

Si=g​h​γi​j​∂∂xj​b=g​hγ​G(i​j)​γ(α⁡(i​j))​∂∂xj​b.S^{i}=gh\gamma^{ij}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}b=\frac{gh}{\gamma}G_{(ij)}\gamma_{(\alpha(ij))}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}b. (16)

Finally, it remains to treat the terms involving Christoffel symbols in (4). It is generally valid the contraction property on repeated indexes for Christoffel symbols of second kind:

Γj​kj=1γ​∂∂xj​γ.\Gamma^{j}_{jk}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\sqrt{\gamma}. (17)

Moreover, for the derivative of the square root of the determinant of the metric it holds

∂∂xk​γ=12​γ​(γ22​∂∂xk​γ11−2​γ12​∂∂xk​γ12+γ11​∂∂xk​γ22).\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\sqrt{\gamma}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\gamma}}\bigg(\gamma_{22}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{11}-2\gamma_{12}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{12}+\gamma_{11}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{22}\bigg). (18)

In (4), it follows that terms involving Christoffel symbols with repeated indexes explicitly read

Γj​kj​Ti​k\displaystyle\Gamma^{j}_{jk}T^{ik} =Ti​k.2​γ​(γ22​∂∂xk​γ11−2​γ12​∂∂xk​γ12+γ11​∂∂xk​γ22),\displaystyle=\frac{T^{ik.}}{2\gamma}\bigg(\gamma_{22}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{11}-2\gamma_{12}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{12}+\gamma_{11}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\gamma_{22}\bigg),

in the mass and in the momentum balances, respectively. Concerning the terms involving the Christoffel symbols with not repeated indexes, by using property (14) with f≡1f\equiv 1 to be applied in definition (5), one can write

Γj​k1​Tk​j=\displaystyle\Gamma^{1}_{jk}T^{kj}= T11γ​γ22​∂∂x1​γ11−2​T11γ​γ12​∂∂x1​γ12+12​γ​(T11​γ11−2​T12​γ12−D22​γ22)​∂∂x1​γ22\displaystyle\frac{T^{11}}{\gamma}\gamma_{22}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}\gamma_{11}-2\frac{T^{11}}{\gamma}\gamma_{12}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}\gamma_{12}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}(T^{11}\gamma_{11}-2T^{12}\gamma_{12}-D^{22}\gamma_{22})\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}\gamma_{22} (20a)

3.2 Final formulation of the governing model

It is now possible to define all the components in (10). The state 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is

𝐐=[h,m1,m2,b,γ11,γ12,γ22]T,\mathbf{Q}=[h,m^{1},m^{2},b,\gamma_{11},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{22}]^{T}, (21)

where the first four entries are the physical variables and the remaining three entries completely describe the covariant metric tensor (that is symmetric and, thus, completely defined by the diagonal terms γ11\gamma_{11} and γ22\gamma_{22} and the extra-diagonal term γ12=γ21\gamma_{12}=\gamma_{21}). Consequently, the dimension mm of the space Ω𝐐\Omega_{\mathbf{Q}} of the admissible states is 7, with the first three variables to be evolved, the bathymetry in fourth position, and the last three components being the metric quantities in covariant representation. Flux 𝐅⁡(𝐐)\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q}) is purely kinetic and it is defined by11 1 Expressions 𝟎a\mathbf{0}_{a} and 𝐎b×c\mathbf{O}_{b\times c}, with a,b,c∈ℕa,b,c\in\mathbb{N}, mean the null vector in ℝa\mathds{R}^{a} and the null matrix in ℝb×c\mathds{R}^{b\times c}, respectively.

(22)

𝐁i(𝐐)=𝐁iη(𝐐)+𝐁im​e​t(𝐐),i=1,2,\mathbf{B}_{i}(\mathbf{Q})=\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\eta}(\mathbf{Q})+\mathbf{B}_{i}^{met}(\mathbf{Q}),\quad i=1,2, (23)

and
